source.description: Label for the indexed content when using single `url` (e.g., 'React useEffect docs', 'Supabase Auth API'). For batch, put source in each requests entry.
Label for this URL's indexed content

requests.description: Batch shape: array of {url, source?} entries. Use with concurrency>1 for parallel fetch. Each request indexed under its own source label. Output preserves input order.

concurrency.description: Max URLs to fetch in parallel (1-8, default: 1). Use 4-8 for I/O-bound multi-URL batches (library docs, changelogs, pricing pages). Capped by os.cpus().length on small machines (response notes when capped). Indexing is always serial regardless — only fetches race.

force.description: Skip cache and re-fetch even if content was recently indexed

ttl.description: Override the cache freshness window for this call, in milliseconds. `ttl: 0` bypasses the cache like `force: true`; omit to use the default 24h TTL.

tools.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search
tools.description:
Search a unified knowledge base with a multi-strategy ranking pipeline. Two parallel matchers run on every query: a Porter-stemming matcher ("caching" finds "cached", "caches", "cach") and a trigram-substring matcher ("useEff" finds "useEffect"). Their ranked lists are merged via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, so a document that ranks well in both surfaces above one that wins only on a single strategy. Multi-term queries get an additional proximity-rerank pass that boosts passages where the query terms appear close together. Typos are corrected via Levenshtein distance and re-searched. Result snippets are window-extracted around the matched terms, not blindly truncated.

The knowledge base is unified: queries reach indexed content you stored (ctx_index, ctx_fetch_and_index, ctx_batch_execute output) AND auto-captured session memory written by hooks (decisions, errors, blockers, plans, user prompts, rejected approaches, tool failures, compaction guides — 26 event categories). File-backed sources carry a content hash and auto-flag staleness when the source file changes.

WHEN:
  - You want to recall something that exists in storage (recently indexed content, prior session events, auto-memory) instead of re-reading raw sources
  - You have multiple related questions about the same body of knowledge — batch every question into one call (the ranking pipeline runs per-query but the round-trip cost is paid once)
  - You want to scope the query to one labelled source (pass `source` — partial match is fine)
  - You want a chronological view across current session + prior sessions + persistent auto-memory (pass `sort: "timeline"` — the default `relevance` mode only ranks within the current session)
  - You want to filter ranked results by content shape (pass `contentType: "code"` to surface implementation snippets or `contentType: "prose"` to surface explanations)

WHEN NOT:
  - The data you want to query has never been stored in the knowledge base AND no session memory has accumulated around it — capture first (run a gather-and-index call), then come back here to query
  - You have one ad-hoc question against data that is not in the knowledge base — answer it inline by running code in the sandbox tool; one round-trip instead of capture-then-query

RETURNS:
  Per-query ranked sections with window-extracted snippets. Use 2-4 specific technical terms per query. Common session-memory source labels: `decision` (user corrections / preferences), `error` and `error-resolution` (past failures + their fixes), `blocker`, `plan`, `user-prompt`, `rejected-approach`, `compaction` (post-compact session guide). See ctx_stats for live category counts.

EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["root cause", "proposed fix", "test coverage"], source: "issue-#683")
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["what did we decide about caching"], source: "decision", sort: "timeline")
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["useEffect cleanup pattern"], source: "react-docs", contentType: "code", limit: 5)
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["last user prompt", "active skills", "open blockers"], sort: "timeline")

source.description: Filter to a specific indexed source (partial match).

contentType.description: Filter results by content type: 'code' or 'prose'.

sort.description: Sort mode. 'relevance' (default): BM25 ranked, current session only. 'timeline': chronological across current session, prior sessions, and auto-memory.

If you found TypeSafe while looking for a model to plug into your coding agent, start here. Jev is **not** a drop-in replacement for the LLM behind Claude Code, Cursor, opencode, Copilot, Muse Spark, Grok Bot, or similar tools. Instead, you can use your coding agent as usual to write code that uses Jev to make decisions.

## 

[​

](#jev-is-not-a-chat-or-code-completion-llm)

Jev is not a chat or code-completion LLM

Jev is a [System One model](/concepts/system-one). It does not generate text, write code, or hold a conversation. It takes a [state](/concepts/state) and a set of typed [questions](/primitives) and returns structured answers your code can use directly:

*   A `choice` from a list of options, with per-option probabilities.
*   A `score` on a rubric you define.
*   A `noul` (0–1) for a true/false statement.

Coding agents rely on an LLM that streams text, calls tools, and edits files based on natural-language instructions. Jev does none of that. There is no `model: "jev-latest"` setting that turns your coding agent into a Jev-powered agent, because the two systems solve different problems.

### jev-gateway > How it works (1)

## How it works

[](#how-it-works)

Jev does not generate text. It answers typed questions about a piece of state (pick one option, give a score, or yes/no) and returns calibrated probabilities with a confidence, in one fast call. Choosing a tool is exactly that kind of question, so the work is split like this:

| Decision | Who makes it |
| --- | --- |
| Which tool, or no tool at all | **Jev** |
| Arguments that are enums, booleans, or constants | **Jev**, in the same call |
| Open-ended arguments such as free text, numbers, and dates | The LLM, already pointed at Jev's tool |
| Plain text replies, and any request without tools | The LLM, untouched |

A request that carries tools triggers one Jev call. The conversation becomes the state, and the questions are: which tool (or none), whether a tool is needed at all (an independent cross-check), and the value of every closed-set argument. The answer selects a mode, which is reported in the `x-jev-gateway-mode` response header:

| Mode | When | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `direct` | Jev is confident about the tool and every argument is an enum, boolean, or constant | The gateway builds the tool call itself, streaming included. **No LLM call.** Never with extended thinking on (Claude Code): the next turn would replay a tool call with no thinking block, which the API rejects, so such a request gets `hint` instead |
| `forced` | Jev is confident about the tool, but some arguments are open-ended | Forwarded with `tool_choic

## [](#one-forward-pass)One forward pass

## How it works

[](#how-it-works)

Jev does not generate text. It answers typed questions about a piece of state (pick one option, give a score, or yes/no) and returns calibrated probabilities with a confidence, in one fast call. Choosing a tool is exactly that kind of question, so the work is split like this:

| --- | --- |
| Which tool, or no tool at all | **Jev** |

| Plain text replies, and any request without tools | The LLM, untouched |

| `forced` | Jev is confident about the tool, but some arguments are open-ended | Forwarded with `tool_choic

## How it works

[](#how-it-works)

Jev does not generate text. It answers typed questions about a piece of state (pick one option, give a score, or yes/no) and returns calibrated probabilities with a confidence, in one fast call. Choosing a tool is exactly that kind of question, so the work is split like this:

| Decision | Who makes it |
| --- | --- |
| Which tool, or no tool at all | **Jev** |
| Arguments that are enums, booleans, or constants | **Jev**, in the same call |
| Open-ended arguments such as free text, numbers, and dates | The LLM, already pointed at Jev's tool |
| Plain text replies, and any request without tools | The LLM, untouched |

The conversation becomes the state, and the questions are: which tool (or none), whether a tool is needed at all (an independent cross-check), and the value of every closed-set argument. ### What is Jev (2026)? TypeSafe AI's System One model > How Jev works[](#how-jev-works)

## How Jev works[](#how-jev-works)

TypeSafe was just as quiet about how Jev got built as it was about what it’s actually running on. Per [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/18/a-new-kind-of-ai-model-from-a-chatgpt-inventor-is-thrilling-developers/), the model was trained entirely on synthetic data over two years in stealth. Almeida still hasn’t said what Jev sits on top of. Outside observers, per the same report, suspect it’s a transformer-based model built on an open-weight LLM, but TypeSafe hasn’t confirmed the architecture either way.

The mechanical diff…

…to sampling.

A chat model generates one token at a time, each conditioned on everything that came before it. This is why a single response can take anywhere from 3 to 329 seconds for today’s frontier models, per TypeSafe’s own published comparisons.

Jev generates every output in a single parallel pass instead: you send it state plus a batch of typed questions, and it scores all of them simultaneously rather than threading them through one token stream.

```

Chat model — sequential, one path at a time

state → [token 1] → [token 2] → [token 3] → … → [token n]

         each token conditioned on every token before it



Jev — parallel, one pass

           ┌→ [question 1] → typed answer + confidence

state ─────┼→ [question 2] → typed answer + confidence

           ├→ [question 3] → typed answer + confidence

           └→ [question n] → typed answer + confidence

         every question scored simultaneously, n

To find the other gateways, the page tries their default ports. A port that never answered is tried again after 10 seconds, then less often, down to once a minute; each try that finds nothing shows as a refused connection in the browser console. Add `?peers=none` to the address to watch only the gateway that serves the page.

**Which inference provider offers prompt caching for long coding-agent sessions?**

The DigitalOcean cache-aware Inference Router can keep an agent session on the model holding its warm cache. That matters for long sessions where repeatedly processing the same context adds cost. Jev is better used for bounded decisions alongside the session than for rewriting its context midstream.

**Which inference platforms offer prompt caching?**

DigitalOcean hosts serving frameworks such as SGLang, which can reuse unchanged context within a model’s serving stack. The cache-aware Inference Router addresses a different problem: preserving a session’s warm cache when routing between models.

**How should I route LLM requests by cost and latency?**

Route narrow tasks such as classification or moderation to a model built for quick, inexpensive decisions, and send open-ended reasoning to a more capable model. Jev fits the first role; The DigitalOcean Inference Router lets you use it alongside other models.

**What should I look for in a low-latency inference provider for a coding agent?**

Look beyond the speed of one model call: tool calls, repeated context processing, and session startup all affect the agent’s response time. DigitalOcean Managed Agents preserve session state when paused and resumed, while Jev can handle narrow decisions within the workflow.

I ran one research iteration. Nothing is filed or written, and the first step to take is an offline AUROC pilot, described at the end.

## What Jev is

"Jev" is TypeSafe's System One decision model. It takes a state and typed questions (`choice`, `score`, `noul` for a 0 to 1 probability) and returns calibrated answers in one forward pass. It generates no text or code. TypeSafe's own docs say it is [not a drop-in for the model behind a coding agent](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/coding-agents). It is a fast classifier that sits beside the agent.

There is already an ecosystem around it:
- **[jev-gateway](https://github.com/vinilana/jev-gateway)** lets Jev pick the tool, plus any enum or boolean arguments, ahead of the LLM. It can skip the LLM call entirely.
- **Open-weight clones** include [agent-jev](https://huggingface.co/aimeigaoshou/agent-jev) (0.6B), mini-Jev and openjev (27B).

## The opening for archy

agent-jev predicts whether a patch passes hidden checks. It scores **57.8% accuracy and 0.589 AUROC** on 1,048 executed coding pairs, which is barely above chance. It also refuses any state over **2,048 tokens**, so it cannot read much of the repo. The coding judgment is the weak part, and the state has to be compact.

That is a gap archy can fill. Its facts are deterministic and compact, and they cost no decoding.

## Candidates, run through the anti-theater gate

| Idea | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **A. Archy features as extra state for a Jev-style patch-passes-checks predictor.** Examples are impact set size, affected tests, layer or cycle verdict, and fan-in of touched modules. | **Pursue.** It is a different kind of test from the six null delivery interventions. The consumer is a classifier, not an agent, and the metric is AUROC. That needs no live agent runs, so the test is cheap. |
| **B. Archy as a label and feature factory.** Use `affected` and `check` verdicts over git history as cheap ground-truth labels to train or evaluate small decision models. | **Pursue, folded into A.** It is the same offline pipeline. |
| **C. Jev as a gate over archy output** (rank violations, replace `check`). | **Reject.** `check` is exact, so a calibrated guess would be worse. `what_to_refactor_next` already ranks. |
| **D. Jev-gateway plus an archy brief in the agent's context.** | **Reject.** This is the seventh "push a fact at the model" idea, and I have no reason it differs from the six that came back null. |
| **E. Jev picking a layer for a new module**, a `choice` over declared layers. | **Park.** I have not checked whether archy's current inference already handles this. |

## What I have not verified

- I did not check whether agent-jev's coding pairs are Python. archy only parses Python, so non-Python pairs would give no features.
- I did not check that the gain exists. A 0.589 baseline is weak, but it could also be near the ceiling for the task.
- The coding-accuracy number is the model card's own figure. I took it as stated.

## Next iteration

Following the "pilot the control before fixing a threshold" rule in AGENTS.md:

1. Pull agent-jev's pair set and see how many are Python.
2. Compute trivial baselines on it (diff size, files touched), because the AUROC to beat is the best simple baseline, not 0.589.
3. Compute archy features for the Python subset.
4. Pre-register the threshold in the repo, then run it.

name: feedback_vet_proposals_anti_theater
description: "vet archy feature proposals against the anti-theater test + OECD axis gate BEFORE filing tickets, especially when motivated by an external paper"

When proposing archy features (tickets, specs, design docs), run them through the
project's own metric-vetting gates BEFORE filing, not after. This applies especially
when the motivation is an external paper or authority (e.g. the 2000 ADL classification
paper), because "an authoritative source says X matters" is precisely the reasoning
those gates exist to distrust.

The two gates, both already documented in-repo:
- **Anti-theater test** (maintainer's PR #142/#143 principle, quoted throughout
  `docs/research/AGENT_CAUSAL_REASONING_SYNTHESIS.md`): *what does an agent or human do
  differently because of this?* A different action, not a different dashboard. A new
  number/axis/synthesis that changes no user action is the "vanity thermometer."
- **OECD four-condition gate** (`docs/research/AXIS_REVIEW.md`), required if a signal
  would reach the score: independence, directionality, actionability, discriminant
  validity. This is what rejected `calls_per_edge` and type-hint coverage as axes.

Also weigh against the maintainer's recorded 2026-05-26 prioritization: the
highest-leverage next move is a **usage signal** (does anyone call archy inside an
agent loop?), not more capability. "More capability" proposals sit below that line
until usage evidence exists.

**Why:** on 2026-07-12 I proposed, filed (#270 typed connectors, #271 conformance),
and merged a spec justified purely by ADL-paper fit, skipping both gates. The user
caught it. The features mostly held up on re-analysis, but the process gap (external
authority -> file -> merge, with no gate) was the real miss.

**How to apply:** before writing a proposal ticket, state explicitly what action an
agent/human takes differently because of the feature; if the answer is "reads a nicer
number," stop or re-scope to the consumer. For any score-reaching signal, run the four
OECD conditions. Prefer tools/packaging a user calls and acts on over new numbers.
Relates to [[feedback_use_deepwork_review]] and [[project_archy_next_up]].

3	description: "vet archy feature proposals against the anti-theater test + OECD axis gate BEFORE filing tickets, especially when motivated by an external paper"

9	
10	When proposing archy features (tickets, specs, design docs), run them through the
11	project's own metric-vetting gates BEFORE filing, not after. This applies especially
12	when the motivation is an external paper or authority (e.g. the 2000 ADL classification
13	paper), because "an authoritative source says X matters" is precisely the reasoning
14	those gates exist to distrust.
15	
16	The two gates, both already documented in-repo:
17	- **Anti-theater test** (maintainer's PR #142/#143 principle, quoted throughout
18	  `docs/research/AGENT_CAUSAL_REASONING_SYNTHESIS.md`): *what does an agent or human do
19	  differently because of this?* A different action, not a different dashboard. A new
20	  number/axis/synthesis that changes no user action is the "vanity thermometer."
21	- **OECD four-condition gate** (`docs/research/AXIS_REVIEW.md`), required if a signal
22	  would reach the score: independence, directionality, actionability, discriminant
23	  validity. This is what rejected `calls_per_edge` and type-hint coverage as axes.
24	
25	Also weigh against the maintainer's recorded 2026-05-26 prioritization: the
26	highest-leverage next move is a **usage signal** (does anyone call archy inside an
27	agent loop?), not more capability. "More capability" proposals sit below that line
28	until usage evidence exists.
29	
30	**Why:** on 2026-07-12 I proposed, filed (#270 typed connectors, #271 conformance),
31	and merged a spec justified purely by ADL-paper fit, skipping both gates. The user
32	caught it. The features mostly held up on re-analysis, but the process gap (external
33	authority -> file -> merge, with no gate) was the real miss.
34	
35	**How to apply:** before writing a proposal ticket, state explicitly what action an
36	agent/human takes differently because of the feature; if the answer is "reads a nicer
37	number," stop or re-scope to the consumer. For any score-reaching signal, run the four
38	OECD conditions. Prefer tools/packaging a user calls and acts on over new numbers.
39	Relates to [[feedback_use_deepwork_review]] and [[project_archy_next_up]].

research(duplicates): use an embedding model as an offline oracle to measure what the AST tiers miss on agent PRs (the Type-4 gap behind #548)
**Problem.** #548 measures how often, and how precisely, a diff-scoped "you re-implemented an existing function" finding fires using archy's shipped detectors (AST-shape hashing plus the token-overlap `near_miss` tier). Its own evidence section says the redundancy agents actually add is mostly Type-4 (semantic, embedding-detected; [arXiv 2601.21276](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21276)), so the shipped detectors are expected to have low recall *by design*, and #548 lists embeddings as a non-goal until they have "their own measured precision gain". Nobody has measured that gain, or how much of the real redundancy sits outside what archy can see. Without it, any feature built on #548 carries an unstated ceiling, and any future "add an embedding tier" idea has no evidence to be judged against.

This ticket measures the gap, offline, and ships nothing.

**Why now and not later.** It reuses #548's dataset extraction and labeling rubric, so the marginal cost is local compute plus a second candidate generator. It also pre-empts the cheaper, wrong way to answer the question: adding an ML dependency to the product because a paper says embeddings find more.

**What changes for the user (the action).** It decides one of three things, each of which changes what gets built:
1. Embedding candidates are precise AND find a substantial share of true redundancy the AST tiers miss: file a feature ticket for an opt-in Type-4 tier (separate, not this one).
2. Embeddings add little: record it in `docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md` and close the line, so nobody re-proposes it.
3. Either way, the measured AST-tier share becomes the stated limit of #548's feature, so its documentation does not over-claim.

**Depends on #548.** Do not start before #548's pre-registration is committed. Reuse its AIDev extraction (base commit, added hunks, per-PR ledger), its 20-PR disjoint pilot split, its scorable-firing rule, and its frozen labeling rubric. Do not build a second harness.

**Design.**
- Candidate generator B, offline only: for each function added in a Python AIDev PR (same size floor as the AST tier), embed it and the base-commit functions of the same repository, take the top-1 nearest neighbour by cosine similarity, and emit it as a candidate if the similarity clears a cutoff.
- **Primary model: `jinaai/jina-embeddings-v2-base-code`** (Apache-2.0, 161M parameters; both verified on its Hugging Face card 2026-10-28). It is the only candidate that could be shipped later without a license problem.
- **Sensitivity model, reported but never decisive: `jinaai/jina-code-embeddings-0.5b`**, a stronger model whose card says `cc-by-nc-4.0` (verified), so bench-only. Its role is to say whether a better embedder would change the verdict, not to decide it.
- Qodo-Embed-1-1.5B is out of scope: its card lists the license as `other`, unverified.
- **Cutoff fixed on the pilot, before any label is read:** choose the similarity that yields the same number of candidates per PR as the shipped AST tiers on the pilot. This compares precision at equal volume and prevents tuning the cutoff against labels.
- **Pooled labeling.** The two labelers see the union of A (AST/near-miss firings from #548) and B (embedding candidates), blind to which generator produced each, under #548's frozen rubric. Report agreement.

**Pre-registered thresholds** (commit in `docs/research/EMBEDDING_ORACLE_RECALL.md` before the harness exists; do not reinterpret afterwards):
- **Scorable floor:** at least 30 scorable labeled candidates from B, from at least 10 repositories. Below it the result is "not measurable at this sample", reported as such, and the line is not extended.
- **Pass (an embedding tier is worth a feature ticket):** B precision at least 0.60 under the primary oracle AND at least 30% of the labeler-TRUE pool is found only by B.
- **Kill:** B precision below 0.40, OR fewer than 10% of the TRUE pool found only by B.
- **Between:** null, not shipped. No post-hoc subgroup rescue; the sensitivity model and any subgroup are reported in full but are not results.
- **Recall is relative to the pooled set, not absolute.** Redundancy that neither generator surfaces is invisible, so "A's share of the TRUE pool" overstates A's true recall. State this in the results and never write it as the detector's recall.

**Harness requirements (AGENTS.md).**
- `bench/embedding_oracle_recall.py`, checkpointed per PR with one ledger row per unit appended in a single write, only `status="ok"` counted done, a crash in one unit never ends the loop, interrupts exit cleanly and say how to resume. Copy the shape of `bench/_supervise.py` and `bench/q1b_run.py`.
- Cache embeddings by function content hash under `bench/cache/` (gitignored). A test that reaches the cache or the model must `skip` when absent: run `mv bench/cache /tmp/bench-cache-aside` before pushing and move it back.
- `--canary` before any real run: a fixture where a loop and a comprehension compute the same thing (Type-4) must be found by B and missed by A; a fixture of two unrelated functions of similar length must not be paired. Assert the fixture reaches each branch before asserting the outcome.
- Verify by mutation: change the cutoff direction, drop the "exists at base" condition, and swap A and B labels in the pooled sample; each must turn a test red. Clear `__pycache__` between mutants.
- Dependencies are bench-only (`uv run --with ...`). Nothing is added to `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` or any runtime import path, and `archy check`, `archy cycles --strict` and `archy conventions . --emit-headers --check` must stay green.
- Drop unmeasurable units; never score them clean.

**Definition of done.** Pre-registration committed first, with its commit hash quoted in the results; canary passes; the 20-PR pilot is reported; the full run completes; results in `bench/embedding_oracle_recall_results.md`; a Study entry in `docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md`, published pass or fail.

**Non-goals.** No embedding dependency in the product. No CLI flag, MCP parameter or hook. Nothing in the score. No live agent runs, so no agent time is spent; the only cost is local CPU. Not a good first issue: it depends on the unfinished #548 harness and needs careful measurement design.

**Evidence limits, stated up front.** My 2026-10-28 search found no clone-detection benchmark (BigCloneBench, POJ-104) reported for either Jina model, so there is no published prior on their precision for this task. That absence is the reason to measure instead of assume. Archy's usage baseline (fewer than 20 real users) means this is research with a decision at the end, not a growth feature; keep it behind #548 in priority.

research(duplicates): use an embedding model as an offline oracle to measure what the AST tiers miss on agent PRs (the Type-4 gap behind #548)
**Problem.** #548 measures how often, and how precisely, a diff-scoped "you re-implemented an existing function" finding fires using archy's shipped detectors (AST-shape hashing plus the token-overlap `near_miss` tier). Its own evidence section says the redundancy agents actually add is mostly Type-4 (semantic, embedding-detected; [arXiv 2601.21276](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21276)), so the shipped detectors are expected to have low recall *by design*, and #548 lists embeddings as a non-goal until they have "their own measured precision gain". Nobody has measured that gain, or how much of the real redundancy sits outside what archy can see. Without it, any feature built on #548 carries an unstated ceiling, and any future "add an embedding tier" idea has no evidence to be judged against.

This ticket measures the gap, offline, and ships nothing.

**Why now and not later.** It reuses #548's dataset extraction and labeling rubric, so the marginal cost is local compute plus a second candidate generator. It also pre-empts the cheaper, wrong way to answer the question: adding an ML dependency to the product because a paper says embeddings find more.

**What changes for the user (the action).** It decides one of three things, each of which changes what gets built:
1. Embedding candidates are precise AND find a substantial share of true redundancy the AST tiers miss: file a feature ticket for an opt-in Type-4 tier (separate, not this one).
2. Embeddings add little: record it in `docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md` and close the line, so nobody re-proposes it.
3. Either way, the measured AST-tier share becomes the stated limit of #548's feature, so its documentation does not over-claim.

**Depends on #548.** Do not start before #548's pre-registration is committed. Reuse its AIDev extraction (base commit, added hunks, per-PR ledger), its 20-PR disjoint pilot split, its scorable-firing rule, and its frozen labeling rubric. Do not build a second harness.

**Design.**
- Candidate generator B, offline only: for each function added in a Python AIDev PR (same size floor as the AST tier), embed it and the base-commit functions of the same repository, take the top-1 nearest neighbour by cosine similarity, and emit it as a candidate if the similarity clears a cutoff.
- **Primary model: `jinaai/jina-embeddings-v2-base-code`** (Apache-2.0, 161M parameters; both verified on its Hugging Face card 2026-10-28). It is the only candidate that could be shipped later without a license problem.
- **Sensitivity model, reported but never decisive: `jinaai/jina-code-embeddings-0.5b`**, a stronger model whose card says `cc-by-nc-4.0` (verified), so bench-only. Its role is to say whether a better embedder would change the verdict, not to decide it.
- Qodo-Embed-1-1.5B is out of scope: its card lists the license as `other`, unverified.
- **Cutoff fixed on the pilot, before any label is read:** choose the similarity that yields the same number of candidates per PR as the shipped AST tiers on the pilot. This compares precision at equal volume and prevents tuning the cutoff against labels.
- **Pooled labeling.** The two labelers see the union of A (AST/near-miss firings from #548) and B (embedding candidates), blind to which generator produced each, under #548's frozen rubric. Report agreement.

**Pre-registered thresholds** (commit in `docs/research/EMBEDDING_ORACLE_RECALL.md` before the harness exists; do not reinterpret afterwards):
- **Scorable floor:** at least 30 scorable labeled candidates from B, from at least 10 repositories. Below it the result is "not measurable at this sample", reported as such, and the line is not extended.
- **Pass (an embedding tier is worth a feature ticket):** B precision at least 0.60 under the primary oracle AND at least 30% of the labeler-TRUE pool is found only by B.
- **Kill:** B precision below 0.40, OR fewer than 10% of the TRUE pool found only by B.
- **Between:** null, not shipped. No post-hoc subgroup rescue; the sensitivity model and any subgroup are reported in full but are not results.
- **Recall is relative to the pooled set, not absolute.** Redundancy that neither generator surfaces is invisible, so "A's share of the TRUE pool" overstates A's true recall. State this in the results and never write it as the detector's recall.

**Harness requirements (AGENTS.md).**
- `bench/embedding_oracle_recall.py`, checkpointed per PR with one ledger row per unit appended in a single write, only `status="ok"` counted done, a crash in one unit never ends the loop, interrupts exit cleanly and say how to resume. Copy the shape of `bench/_supervise.py` and `bench/q1b_run.py`.
- Cache embeddings by function content hash under `bench/cache/` (gitignored). A test that reaches the cache or the model must `skip` when absent: run `mv bench/cache /tmp/bench-cache-aside` before pushing and move it back.
- `--canary` before any real run: a fixture where a loop and a comprehension compute the same thing (Type-4) must be found by B and missed by A; a fixture of two unrelated functions of similar length must not be paired. Assert the fixture reaches each branch before asserting the outcome.
- Verify by mutation: change the cutoff direction, drop the "exists at base" condition, and swap A and B labels in the pooled sample; each must turn a test red. Clear `__pycache__` between mutants.
- Dependencies are bench-only (`uv run --with ...`). Nothing is added to `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` or any runtime import path, and `archy check`, `archy cycles --strict` and `archy conventions . --emit-headers --check` must stay green.
- Drop unmeasurable units; never score them clean.

**Definition of done.** Pre-registration committed first, with its commit hash quoted in the results; canary passes; the 20-PR pilot is reported; the full run completes; results in `bench/embedding_oracle_recall_results.md`; a Study entry in `docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md`, published pass or fail.

**Non-goals.** No embedding dependency in the product. No CLI flag, MCP parameter or hook. Nothing in the score. No live agent runs, so no agent time is spent; the only cost is local CPU. Not a good first issue: it depends on the unfinished #548 harness and needs careful measurement design.

**Evidence limits, stated up front.** My 2026-10-28 search found no clone-detection benchmark (BigCloneBench, POJ-104) reported for either Jina model, so there is no published prior on their precision for this task. That absence is the reason to measure instead of assume. Archy's usage baseline (fewer than 20 real users) means this is research with a decision at the end, not a growth feature; keep it behind #548 in priority.

Jev is TypeSafe's "System One" model: state plus typed questions (choice, score, noul) in, calibrated probabilities out, no decoding. Open clones exist (agent-jev 0.6B, mini-Jev, openjev 27B). It is not a coding LLM and TypeSafe says so. jev-gateway lets it pick tools ahead of the LLM.

Reviewed 2026-11-06, five ideas, none survived:
- **Archy features into a patch-passes-checks predictor**: agent-jev's coding_gates data is 2,100 recorded test runs (diff plus test output), not repo checkouts, so no module graph to compute features on. Archy's gated events are also ~0.5% of commits (near-zero variance), and the one feature with variance (impact size) is a diff-size proxy. Needs no Jev at all if it were tried.
- **Archy verdicts as training labels**: predicting what `check`/`affected` compute exactly is theater; run the tool.
- **Jev as a gate or ranker over archy output**: `check` is exact, `what_to_refactor_next` already ranks.
- **Jev deciding when to call archy / pushing a brief via the gateway**: the seventh delivery-line idea (see [[project_archy_local_model_line]]), no reason it differs from the six nulls.
- **Jev picking a layer for a new module**: `check`/`simulate` verify placement exactly anyway.

Only weak adjacent link: a calibrated "same behavior?" judge could be one more labeler-assist for #587 (embedding oracle for Type-4 duplicates). It changes no decision there, so it was not added.

**Why:** [[feedback_vet_proposals_anti_theater]] and the <20 users baseline ([[project_archy_usage_baseline]]) put integration work with a niche gateway below the usage-signal priority.
**How to apply:** if Jev comes up again, start from this list; a new idea needs a stated action an agent or human takes differently that `check`, `simulate` or `affected` do not already cause. Possible parked packaging check: whether archy's MCP tool descriptions route well under a 0.6B tool router (archy tools take open-ended path args, so the gateway would use `forced` mode, not `direct`). Not filed.

content.text:
Tree-sitter artifacts as Jev state fail the same gate, so I filed nothing. archy depends on `tree-sitter-python`, so its parse artifacts are real. They are function nodes, import edges, AST-shape hashes and complexity. Here is each way they could feed Jev:

| Use | Verdict | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Compress a big diff into a skeleton (signatures, changed symbols, import edges) so it fits Jev's 2,048-token ceiling** | Not an archy ticket | This is the only new idea. It would help Jev users, but any tree-sitter user can build it. archy's parser is Python-only. |
| | | The compression only matters if Jev's judgments improve with more input, and agent-jev's 0.589 AUROC suggests they may not. |
| | | You could measure it offline on agent-jev's 2,100 recorded runs. That tests Jev clones, not archy, and the runs are test output rather than parseable repos. |
| **Feed complexity or hotspot numbers to Jev's `score` primitive** | Dead | A number goes in and a number comes out. Nobody acts differently. |
| **Extract function bodies for a "same behavior?" judge** | Dead | archy's duplicate detectors already extract these. The judge adds nothing to #587's decision, as before. |
| **Tag each module with a semantic role to propose layers** | Dead | This is idea E again. `archy conventions` and the dependency matrix already derive layering from the actual import graph, and a guess from names would be weaker. |

I appended this to the memory note `project_archy_jev_review.md`.

If you want the skeleton idea pursued, it belongs upstream with the agent-jev authors. I would only open an issue there if you ask, since that posts outside your repo.

content.content:
fix(cycles,score): a scan that found 0 internal modules reports a clean pass
**The gap.** When a scan yields 0 internal modules, `archy cycles --strict` prints `# No cycles found (min_size=2).` and exits 0 (`_cycles_to_text`, `src/archy/cli.py:3230`), and `--format json` prints a bare `[]`. `archy score` prints `archy score: 1.000` with every axis at 1.000. Reproduced on main (f6fb600) with:
- an empty directory;
- a flat scripts directory where `a.py` does `import b` and `b.py` does `import a`, a real import cycle that scans to 0 modules (no `__init__.py`), so `--strict` passes over it;
- `exclude: ['**']` in `archy.yaml`.

`score` already prints `# graph: 0 modules, 0 edges` and has `inputs.module_count: 0` in JSON, so the defect is the headline 1.000. It also poisons `score --strict`, which compares against the last recorded score: a vacuous 1.000 reads as an improvement.

**Anti-theater.** A CI step or pre-commit hook pointed at the wrong directory goes red or says why, instead of staying green forever. This is AGENTS.md's "a rule set that cannot fire looks exactly like a clean codebase" applied to the two gates that still say nothing; `check` already qualifies its verdict by coverage (#362, #404).

**Scope (agreed).**
- `cycles` text: on 0 modules, say `# 0 internal modules scanned under <path>; nothing was checked` instead of "No cycles found".
- `cycles --strict`: exit non-zero on 0 modules, with the reason on stderr.
- `score`: on 0 modules, state it in text, and add an additive field (for example `modules_scanned`) to `_score_to_dict` (`src/archy/cli.py:2040`) and `ScorePayload` (`src/archy/mcp.py:306`). Assert on `model_dump()`.
- No warn|error config mode; there is no frequency data to justify one.

**Open design points.** The reviewers disagree on three things; settle them in the PR description:
1. Cycles JSON and MCP shape. `_cycles_to_json` (`cli.py:2606`) and `archy_cycles` (`mcp.py:762`, returns `list[Cycle]`) are bare lists. One reviewer adds a `modules_scanned` field anyway; the other says that is a breaking shape change and proposes stderr for CLI JSON and a `ToolError` on 0 modules for MCP, with any shape change filed separately. def run_score(
    path: Path,
    *,
    internal_only: bool,
    record: bool,
    strict: bool,
    strict_tolerance: float,
) -> ScorePayload:
    if not 0.0 <= strict_tolerance <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError(f"strict_tolerance must be in [0, 1]; got {strict_tolerance}")

    graph = _load_graph(path, internal_only=internal_only)
    score = compute_score(graph)
    history_path = path / ".archy" / "history.jsonl"

    gate: ScoreGate | None = None
    if strict:
        rows = read_history(history_path)
        if rows:
            previous = rows[-1]
            delta = score.overall - previous.overall
            gate = ScoreGate(
                previous=previous.overall,
                previous_commit=previous.commit,
                previous_timestamp=previous.timestamp,
                current=score.overall,
                delta=delta,
                tolerance=strict_tolerance,
                passed=delta >= -strict_tolerance,
            )
        else:
            gate = ScoreGate(
                previous=None,
                current=score.overall,
                delta=None,
                tolerance=strict_tolerance,
                passed=True,
            )

    if record:
        commit, branch = git_metadata(path)
        append_history(history_path, row_from_score(score, commit=commit, branch=branch))

    return ScorePayload(
        overall=score.overall,
        components=score_components(score),
        inputs=score.inputs,
        gate=gate,
    )

"""Composite architecture quality score over an import graph.

Five sub-metrics, each in [0, 1], aggregated via geometric mean so a
weak score on any axis pulls the overall down hard:

* modularity: Newman's Q over a greedy community partition,
              normalized as (Q + 0.5) / 1.5 to map [-0.5, 1.0] -> [0, 1].
* acyclicity: 1 - tangle_ratio, where tangle_ratio is the fraction of nodes
              that sit inside an SCC of size >= 2 (or a self-looped singleton).
              A small isolated cycle in a large codebase is a smaller pathology
              than the same cycle dominating a small codebase; the ratio
              captures that. cycle_count is preserved as a diagnostic.
...
                  compute_modularity_weighted, compute_score
archy:mirrored-by ScoreInputs -> archy.diff, archy.mcp_payloads,
                  compute_acyclicity -> bench.call_weighted_modularity, bench.dsm,
                  compute_complexity -> archy.diff, bench.call_weighted_modularity,
                  bench.dsm, compute_depth -> bench.call_weighted_modularity,
                  bench.dsm, compute_equality -> bench.call_weighted_modularity,
                  bench.dsm, compute_modularity -> bench.call_weighted_modularity,
                  bench.dsm, compute_score -> archy.cli, archy.diff, archy.mcp_runs,
                  bench.inloop_prevalence, bench.q1b_score
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import networkx as nx
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

from archy.cycles import find_cycles
from archy.reach import compute_propagation_cost


VACUOUS_SCORE_NOTE = (
    "0 internal modules scanned; the overall of 1.000 is vacuous and nothing was scored"
)
"""Said wherever a score over zero modules is shown (#523).

`overall` stays numeric so existing consumers and history rows keep parsing; this
note is how the reason travels with it on every surface.
"""


class ScoreInputs(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    module_count: int
    edge_count: int
    cycle_count: int
    tangle_ratio: float
    max_depth: int
    community_count: int
    raw_modularity: float
    raw_gini: float

def test_python_m_entry_point_reaches_the_header_helpers(tmp_path: Path):

    The `__main__` guard used to sit above `_require_headers_flags`, so this
    command died with a NameError instead of printing the usage error the
    console script prints (#782).
    """
    project = _make_empty_package_project(tmp_path)
    (project / "pkg" / "a.py").write_text("X = 1\n")
    r = subprocess.run(
        [sys.executable, "-m", "archy.cli", "conventions", str(project), "--write"],

def _call_tool(server, name: str, args: dict) -> tuple[list, dict | None]:
    """Call a tool in-process and return `(content, structured)` on either SDK major.

    mcp 1.x returns that pair directly; 2.0 returns a `CallToolResult` instead.
    Normalized here rather than at each call site, and `structuredContent` is read
    from the wire form because 2.0 also renamed the attribute (see
    `archy.mcp_compat`).

    These in-process calls poke the SDK's own surface, which is why they are the
    only part of this file a major bump touches. The protocol-level contract is
    covered by `tests/test_mcp_protocol.py`, which speaks stdio and passes
    unchanged on both majors.
    """
    result = asyncio.run(server.call_tool(name, args))
    if isinstance(result, tuple):  # mcp 1.x
        return result
    return result.content, result.model_dump(by_alias=True).get("structuredContent")


def _output_schema(tool) -> dict | None:
    """Read `outputSchema` from the wire form, not the Python attribute.

    mcp 2.0 renamed every model attribute to snake_case (`outputSchema` ->
    `output_schema`) while keeping the serialization aliases identical, so
    attribute access breaks across the major and the protocol does not. Dumping
    by alias is both version-agnostic and closer to what a client actually
    parses. See `archy.mcp_compat`.
    """

    assert isinstance(result, list)  # exclusion is off, so the bare-list shape
    [cycle] = result
    assert sorted(cycle.modules) == ["pkg.a", "pkg.b"]
    edge = cycle.edges[0]
    assert edge.source and edge.target

def _call_tool(server, name: str, args: dict) -> tuple[list, dict | None]:
    """Call a tool in-process and return `(content, structured)` on either SDK major.

    mcp 1.x returns that pair directly; 2.0 returns a `CallToolResult` instead.
    Normalized here rather than at each call site, and `structuredContent` is read
    from the wire form because 2.0 also renamed the attribute (see
    `archy.mcp_compat`).

    These in-process calls poke the SDK's own surface, which is why they are the
    only part of this file a major bump touches. The protocol-level contract is
    covered by `tests/test_mcp_protocol.py`, which speaks stdio and passes
    unchanged on both majors.
    """
    result = asyncio.run(server.call_tool(name, args))
    if isinstance(result, tuple):  # mcp 1.x

    return result.content, result.model_dump(by_alias=True).get("structuredContent")

"""A scan that found 0 internal modules checked nothing, and must say so (#523).

`cycles` printed "No cycles found" and `score` printed 1.000 over an empty
directory, over a flat scripts directory holding a real import cycle, and over a
config that excludes everything. Each case is paired with a control that
scans real modules, so a guard that fires on everything goes red too.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
from collections.abc import Callable
from pathlib import Path

import pytest
from click.testing import CliRunner

from archy.cli import main
from archy.mcp import create_server
from archy.mcp_compat import ToolError
from archy.mcp_runs import run_cycles, run_score
from archy.score import VACUOUS_SCORE_NOTE
from tests.test_mcp import _call_tool


def _empty_dir(root: Path) -> Path:
    return root


def _scripts_cycle(root: Path) -> Path:
    """A real import cycle that scans to 0 modules: no `__init__.py`, so no package."""
    (root / "a.py").write_text("import b\n")
    (root / "b.py").write_text("import a\n")
    return root


def _excluded_everything(root: Path) -> Path:
    pkg = root / "pkg"
    pkg.mkdir()
    (pkg / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    (pkg / "a.py").write_text("X = 1\n")
    (root / "archy.yaml").write_text("exclude: ['**']\n")
    return root


def _real_package(root: Path) -> Path:
    pkg = root / "pkg"
    pkg.mkdir()
    (pkg / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    (pkg / "a.py").write_text("from pkg import b\n")
    (pkg / "b.py").write_text("X = 1\n")
    return root

def empty_project(request: pytest.FixtureRequest, tmp_path: Path) -> Path:
    project = request.param(tmp_path)
    # Assert the fixture reaches the branch before asserting the verdict: a
    # fixture that drifts to scan a module would make every test below vacuous.
    graph = CliRunner().invoke(main, ["graph", str(project), "--internal-only"])
    assert graph.output.startswith("# 0 internal module(s)"), graph.output
    return project


@pytest.fixture
def real_project(tmp_path: Path) -> Path:
    project = _real_package(tmp_path)
    graph = CliRunner().invoke(main, ["graph", str(project), "--internal-only"])
    assert not graph.output.startswith("# 0 internal module(s)"), graph.output
    return project

    assert VACUOUS_SCORE_NOTE in result.output.splitlines()[0]


def test_score_json_carries_the_reason_and_keeps_overall_numeric(empty_project: Path):
    result = CliRunner().invoke(main, ["score", str(empty_project), "--format", "json"])
    payload = json.loads(result.stdout)

    assert payload["modules_scanned"] == 0
    assert payload["note"] == VACUOUS_SCORE_NOTE

def test_run_score_refuses_to_record_or_gate_over_nothing(empty_project: Path, flag: str):
    kwargs = {"record": False, "strict": False, "strict_tolerance": 0.02, flag: True}
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="nothing was scored"):

    ).model_dump()
    assert payload["modules_scanned"] > 0
    assert payload["note"] is None

Base directory for this skill: /Users/hosanglee/.claude/plugins/cache/deepwork-plugins/deepwork/0.14.0/skills/review

# DeepWork Review

Run automated code reviews on the current branch based on `.deepreview` config files.

## Routing — Check Before Proceeding

**STOP and redirect** if either of these applies:

- User wants to **configure, create, or modify** review rules (e.g., "add a security review", "set up reviews for our API layer") → use the `configure_reviews` skill instead
- User wants to **add a doc-sync rule** (keep a documentation file in sync with source files) → call `start_workflow` with `job_name="deepwork_reviews"` and `workflow_name="add_document_update_rule"`

Only proceed past this section if the user wants to **run** reviews.

## Pre-flight — Verify Agent Availability

Before running reviews, check that the `deepwork:reviewer` agent is available. If it does not appear in the agents list (i.e., the Agent tool does not list `deepwork:reviewer` as a valid `subagent_type`), **STOP** and tell the user:

> The `deepwork:reviewer` agent is not available. Please run `/reload-plugins` to pick up the latest plugin updates, then try again.

Do not proceed with reviews until the agent is available.

## How to Run

1. Call the `mcp__deepwork__get_review_instructions` tool directly:
   - **No arguments** to review the current branch's changes (auto-detects via git diff against the main branch).
   - **With `files`** to review only specific files: `mcp__deepwork__get_review_instructions(files=["src/app.py", "src/lib.py"])`. When provided, only reviews whose include/exclude patterns match the given files will be returned. Use this when the user asks to review a particular file or set of files rather than the whole branch.
   - **If the result says no rules are configured**: Ask the user if they'd like to auto-discover and set up rules. If yes, invoke the `/deepwork` skill with the `deepwork_reviews` job's `discover_rules` workflow. Stop here — do not proceed with running reviews if there are no rules.
2. The output will list review tasks to invoke in parallel. Each task has `description`, `subagent_type`, and `prompt` fields — these map directly to the Agent tool parameters. Launch all of them as parallel agents.
3. **While review agents run**, check for a changelog and open PR (see below).
4. Collect the results from all review agents.

## Changelog & PR Description Check

Run this concurrently with the review agents (step 2 above) — don't wait for reviews to finish first.

1. Check if the project has a changelog file (e.g., `CHANGELOG.md`, `CHANGELOG`, `CHANGES.md`).
2. If a changelog exists and there are commits on the current branch beyond the main branch:
   - Read the changelog and the branch's commit log (`git log main..HEAD --oneline`).
   - Verify the changelog's unreleased/current section accurately reflects what the branch does. If entries are missing, outdated, or inaccurate, update the changelog.
3. If a PR is open for the current branch (check with `gh pr view`):
   - If you updated the changelog, also verify the PR description matches. Update it with `gh pr edit` if needed.
   - If the changelog was already accurate, skip the PR description check.

## Acting on Results

For each finding from the review agents:

- **Obviously good changes with no downsides** (e.g., fixing a typo, removing an unused import, adding a missing null check): make the change immediately without asking. When in doubt, ask.
- **Everything else** (refactors, style changes, architectural suggestions, anything with trade-offs):
  1. Use AskUserQuestion to ask the user about each finding **individually**. Do not group issues together unless they are the same issue occurring in multiple files; otherwise, use AskUserQuestion to ask about each issue separately. This lets the user make separate decisions on each item.
  2. For each question, provide several concrete fix approaches as options when there are reasonable alternatives (e.g., "Update the spec to match the code" vs "Update the code to match the spec" vs "Skip").
  3. If a finding seems minor or debatable, include an option to suppress that error in the future — such as a clarification to the rule if it is too narrow, or a comment on the offending content if comments work in that context.
  4. Be concise — quote the key finding, don't dump the full review.

When a finding is dismissed (user chooses "Skip" or you determine it's not actionable for this PR), call `mcp__deepwork__mark_review_as_passed` with the review's ID so it won't re-run on subsequent iterations.

## Iterate

After making any changes:

1. Call `mcp__deepwork__get_review_instructions` with `files` set to **only the files you edited** during this iteration. This scopes the re-review to your changes rather than re-reviewing the entire branch.
2. Repeat the cycle (run → act on results → run again) until a clean run — one where all review agents return no findings, or all remaining findings have been explicitly skipped by the user.
3. On subsequent runs, you only need to re-run tasks that had findings last time — skip tasks that were clean.
4. Reviews that already passed are automatically skipped as long as reviewed files remain unchanged.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
